title: Agent architecture
summary: Architecture starts with whether you need an agent at all: Anthropic recommends the simplest solution that works. When you do, a lead agent with parallel subagents suits broad, valuable research, and long-running agents need memory that lives outside the context window.
keyPoints: Find the **simplest solution**; optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough for many apps.
Multi-agent systems excel at **breadth-first**, parallelizable work, but use about **15×** the tokens of a chat (single agents about 4×).
Each subagent needs an **objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear task boundaries**.
Long-horizon options: **compaction** for back-and-forth, **structured notes** for milestones, **sub-agents** for parallel research.
Across sessions, a **progress file plus git history** (and a JSON feature list) lets a fresh agent pick up the work.

sections.heading: Start simple, or skip the agent
sections.body:
When building with LLMs, Anthropic recommends finding the simplest solution possible and only increasing complexity when needed. This might mean not building agentic systems at all. Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance.

When more complexity is warranted, workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks, and agents fit when flexibility and model-driven decisions are needed at scale. For many applications, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.

sections.heading: Lead agents and subagents
sections.body:
Anthropic's Research feature uses an orchestrator-worker design: a lead agent analyzes the query, develops a strategy and spawns subagents that search in parallel, each with its own context window, then condense what they found for the lead agent.

This works best for breadth-first queries with many independent directions. It costs more: agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chats, and multi-agent systems about 15×. Domains where all agents must share the same context, or with many dependencies between agents, are not a good fit today.

The lead agent must teach its subagents well. Each needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; otherwise they duplicate work or leave gaps. Scaling rules help too: simple fact-finding needs just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls.

diagram.caption: The Research system: plan, search in parallel, synthesize, cite.

sections.heading: Memory for long-running agents
sections.body:
When a task outgrows one context window, Anthropic describes three techniques:

- Compaction: summarize a conversation nearing the limit and restart with the summary; it suits extensive back-and-forth
- Structured note-taking: the agent writes notes outside the context window and reads them back later; it suits iterative development with clear milestones
- Sub-agent architectures: focused sub-agents with clean context windows return condensed summaries; they suit complex research

For coding across many sessions, Anthropic found compaction alone wasn't sufficient. An initializer agent sets up an init.sh script, a claude-progress.txt log, an initial git commit and a JSON feature list with every feature marked failing. Each later session reads the progress file and git log, works on one feature, and ends with a commit and a progress update.

title: Building agents with the Agent SDK
summary: The Claude Agent SDK gives you the tools, agent loop and context management behind Claude Code, as a Python or TypeScript library in a process you run. You shape the loop with turn and budget caps, permission rules and hooks, and extend it with custom tools and subagents. Managed Agents is the hosted alternative.
keyPoints: The loop repeats until Claude replies with **no tool calls**; `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` cap it, and both default to no limit.
Check `ResultMessage.subtype`: `result` exists only on `success`; limits give `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd`.
`allowed_tools` **pre-approves** and does not constrain `bypassPermissions`; `disallowed_tools` blocks, even in that mode.
`PreToolUse` hooks run before a tool and can deny it; if any hook returns deny, the operation is blocked.
A subagent gets only the **Agent tool's prompt** from its parent, and only its final message returns.

sections.heading: What the Agent SDK gives you
sections.body:
The Agent SDK embeds the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code in your own application. It includes built-in tools (read, write and edit files, run commands, search the web), hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions and sessions.

Pick the option by who runs the agent:

- Agent SDK: Claude Code's agent in a process you operate
- Client SDK: direct Claude API access; you write the tool loop yourself or use the beta tool runner
- Managed Agents: Anthropic hosts the agent harness, with sessions in a managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox

Self-hosting the SDK means running a long-lived `claude` subprocess per session, with transcripts on local disk that don't survive a container restart unless you configure a SessionStore. Managed Agents is in beta and is built around agents, environments, sessions and events.

sections.heading: The loop and its limits
sections.body:
Claude evaluates the prompt, calls tools, receives the results and repeats. Each round trip is one turn, and the loop ends when Claude produces a response with no tool calls. The SDK then yields a `ResultMessage` with the final text, token usage, cost and session ID.

Without limits the loop runs until Claude finishes, which can run long on open-ended prompts. Cap it with `max_turns` (tool-use turns) or `max_budget_usd`; setting a budget is a good default for production agents. When a cap is hit, the result subtype is `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd` and there is no `result` field, so check the subtype first. Every result carries `session_id`, so you can resume.

sections.heading: Permissions and hooks
sections.body:
Hooks run first, then deny rules, then ask rules, then the permission mode, then allow rules, and finally your `canUseTool` callback. A deny rule blocks a tool even in `bypassPermissions` mode, and a bare deny such as `Bash` removes the tool from Claude's context.

`allowed_tools` only pre-approves. With `bypassPermissions`, unlisted tools are still approved, so block tools there with `disallowed_tools`. Calls auto-approved earlier never reach `canUseTool`.

Hooks are callbacks at points in the loop. `PreToolUse` fires before a tool executes and can allow, deny or modify the call; a `permissionDecisionReason` tells the model why. `PostToolUse` fires on the result, and `Stop` when execution stops. Hooks run in your application process, so they don't consume context.

sections.heading: Custom tools and subagents
sections.body:
A custom tool has a name, description, input schema and handler, wrapped in an in-process MCP server and named `mcp__{server_name}__{tool_name}`. A handler error doesn't stop the loop; return `isError: true` to compose the message Claude reads.

Subagents isolate context, run in parallel, and can have their own prompt, tools and model. A non-fork subagent starts fresh: the only content passed from the parent is the Agent tool's prompt, and only its final message returns as the tool result.

title: Workflow patterns
summary: Anthropic's Building effective agents post describes five workflow patterns built from an augmented LLM, from fixed prompt chains to feedback loops, and then agents that direct themselves. Choose the simplest pattern that fits; the post advises starting with direct API calls rather than a framework.
keyPoints: **Prompt chaining**: fixed steps, each call using the previous output, with optional gates; trades latency for accuracy.
**Routing**: classify the input, then send it to a specialized prompt, tool set or model.
**Parallelization**: sectioning splits independent subtasks; voting repeats the same task for diverse outputs.
**Orchestrator-workers**: a central LLM decides subtasks per input. **Evaluator-optimizer**: generate, critique, refine in a loop.
The post advises starting with **LLM APIs directly**; if you use a framework, understand the underlying code.

sections.heading: The building block and frameworks
sections.body:
The basic building block is an augmented LLM: an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. The Model Context Protocol is one way to implement these augmentations.

Frameworks make it easy to start by simplifying low-level tasks like calling LLMs, defining and parsing tools, and chaining calls. The December 2024 post named several, including the Claude Agent SDK, though it notes the tooling landscape has since changed. It warns that frameworks can add abstraction that obscures the underlying prompts and responses, making them harder to debug. The post suggests starting with LLM APIs directly, understanding any framework's underlying code, and reducing abstraction layers as you move to production.

sections.heading: Five workflow patterns
sections.body:
- Prompt chaining: a sequence of steps, each LLM call processing the previous output, with optional programmatic gates; for tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks
- Routing: classify an input and direct it to a specialized follow-up; for distinct categories that are better handled separately
- Parallelization: sectioning runs independent subtasks in parallel; voting runs the same task several times for diverse outputs
- Orchestrator-workers: a central LLM breaks down the task, delegates to workers and synthesizes results; for tasks where you can't predict the subtasks
- Evaluator-optimizer: one LLM call generates while another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop; for clear criteria where iterative refinement adds measurable value

sections.heading: Agents and environment feedback
sections.body:
Agents are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop. During execution, the agent must gain ground truth from the environment at each step, such as tool call results or code execution, to assess its progress. It can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when it hits blockers.

Coding agents work well because code is verifiable through automated tests, and agents can iterate using test results as feedback. Because agents mean higher costs and the potential for compounding errors, Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails. Add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.

title: Building a production agent
summary: Decide workflow or agent before you write code: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance. An agent is a pattern, Claude using tools in a loop, and the wiring path (a raw Messages API loop, the Agent SDK or Claude Managed Agents) only decides who runs that loop. On every path you register tools, set a system prompt, handle the loop and define exit conditions.
keyPoints: **Workflows** follow predefined code paths; **agents** direct their own process. Agentic systems often trade **latency and cost** for better task performance.
The agent is the **pattern**; the wiring path is an implementation choice about who runs the loop and what you build yourself.
Raw loop: continue while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`. Agent SDK: built-in loop in a **process you operate**. Managed Agents: Anthropic hosts the harness.
Four steps on every path: **register tools**, **set the system prompt**, **handle the tool-use loop**, **define exit conditions**.
SDK limits `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` default to **no limit**; a budget is a good default for production agents.
Human checkpoints belong in the design: in the SDK, `canUseTool` **pauses execution** until your app returns allow or deny.

sections.heading: Workflow or agent: decide first
sections.body:
A **workflow** is a system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. An **agent** is a system where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool usage. Agents are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop.

Make this call before the first line of code: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and you should consider when that tradeoff makes sense. Anthropic recommends finding the simplest solution possible and only increasing complexity when needed:

- Workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks.
- Agents are the better option when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed at scale.
sections.example: Invoice intake where every document goes extract → validate → save is a **workflow**: the steps never change, so fixed code paths are cheaper and predictable. A bug-fixing assistant that can't know in advance which files it must read or how many attempts it needs is an **agent**: it needs to decide its own next step from what each tool returns.

sections.heading: Three wiring paths: who runs the loop
sections.body:
The agent is the pattern; the **wiring path** is an implementation choice about who runs the loop and what you take on.

- **Raw Messages API loop**: you call the API from a client SDK and write the tool loop yourself (or let the SDK's beta tool runner drive it). You get direct model access and fine-grained control, and you own tool execution, history and every exit check.
- **Claude Agent SDK**: a Python or TypeScript library that gives you the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, with permissions, sessions and hooks. It runs in a process you operate.
- **Claude Managed Agents**: a hosted agent harness that runs the loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox. Best for long-running tasks and asynchronous work; it's in beta and needs the `managed-agents-2026-04-01` header (the SDK sets it).
sections.example: A team wants exact control over when each tool runs and how results are fed back, and is happy to build the loop: **raw Messages API**. A team wants Claude Code's file, shell and web tools inside its own Python service: **Agent SDK**. A team wants hour-long jobs in a cloud sandbox with no loop or sandbox of its own to run: **Managed Agents**.

sections.heading: The four steps that hold on every path
sections.body:
Whichever path you choose, the same four steps define the agent:

- **Register tools**: the `tools` array on the raw API; built-in tools plus custom tools and MCP servers in the SDK; the tools listed in a Managed Agents agent definition.
- **Set the system prompt**: the `system` parameter on the raw API. In the SDK, leaving `systemPrompt` unset gives a minimal prompt covering tool calling only; the `claude_code` preset (optionally with `append`) gives Claude Code's prompt; a custom string replaces it entirely.
- **Handle the tool-use loop**: on the raw API, run each `tool_use` request and send back `tool_result` blocks. In the SDK, the SDK runs each tool and feeds results back without returning control to your code.
- **Define exit conditions**: decide what ends a run, both on success and when a limit is hit.

diagram.caption: The raw-API loop: repeat while stop_reason is tool_use.

sections.heading: Exit conditions
sections.body:
A **stopping condition** ends the loop even if the task isn't finished, such as a maximum number of iterations. It's common to include them to maintain control.

- **Raw API**: the loop exits on any stop reason other than `"tool_use"` (`"end_turn"`, `"max_tokens"`, `"stop_sequence"` or `"refusal"`), and your code adds any iteration cap.
- **Agent SDK**: the loop ends when Claude replies with no tool calls. `max_turns` caps tool-use round trips and `max_budget_usd` caps estimated spend; both default to no limit. Hitting one returns a `ResultMessage` with `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd`, and `result` is only present on `success`.

Spend is compared with the cap after each response arrives, so the response that reaches it still completes. Leave headroom when you set the cap.
sections.example: `max_turns=30` stops a runaway refactor. Your code then checks `message.subtype`: on `"success"` it reads `message.result`; on `"error_max_turns"` it saves `session_id` so the session can be resumed with a higher limit.

sections.heading: Orchestration and human checkpoints
sections.body:
**Orchestration** in the SDK means a main agent delegating to **subagents**. Each runs in its own conversation, and only its final message returns to the parent, so subtasks don't flood the main context and independent ones can run in parallel. Unless the subagent is a fork, the only content passed in is the Agent tool's prompt string.

A **human-in-the-loop checkpoint** is a point where the agent pauses for a person. Agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers, so decide where those checkpoints go while you design the agent. In the SDK:

- A `canUseTool` callback fires when a tool isn't auto-approved and pauses execution until you return allow or deny.
- Auto-approved calls (an allow rule, `acceptEdits`, `bypassPermissions`) never reach it; for a check on every call, use a `PreToolUse` hook.
- Claude's own clarifying questions arrive through `AskUserQuestion`.

In Managed Agents you can send events to steer a session or interrupt it.
sections.example: A cleanup agent may run `Read` and `Grep` freely, but every `Bash` call must reach `canUseTool`, which shows the command in your UI. If the user rejects `rm -rf build/`, you return deny with the message "User wants files archived, not deleted", and Claude reads it and adjusts.

title: Agent memory and Skills
summary: An agent can remember in four ways: in the context window, in external storage such as the memory tool, as a compacted summary, or not at all. The right choice depends on task characteristics: how long the work lasts and what must survive it. Skills add reusable instructions that load only when used, and a subagent gets a skill's content at startup only if its `skills` field lists it.
keyPoints: **In-context** memory is the history you send; the Messages API is stateless, so you always send the full conversation.
**External storage**: the memory tool keeps files under `/memories` across conversations, on storage **your application** controls.
**Summarized** memory (compaction) frees space but may drop early instructions; standing rules belong in CLAUDE.md, re-injected every request.
Skills: the **description** is always in context; the **full body** loads only when invoked.
CLAUDE.md is for every-session facts (target under **200 lines**); a repeated multi-step procedure belongs in a skill.
A subagent doesn't see skills you invoked; list them in its **`skills`** field to preload. Removing the **`Skill`** tool blocks skills.

sections.heading: In-context memory and stateless agents
sections.body:
**In-context memory** is whatever sits in the context window: the conversation history plus tool inputs and outputs. The Messages API is **stateless**: it keeps nothing between calls, so you always send the full conversational history. In the Agent SDK the context window doesn't reset between turns within a session; everything accumulates, including large tool outputs.

In-context memory ends with the conversation, and it grows with every turn.

**No persistent memory (stateless)** means each request or session starts fresh with nothing carried over. Each Claude Code session, for example, begins with a fresh context window. This is the right choice when every request stands alone.
sections.example: A classifier that labels each incoming email on its own needs no memory: each request holds one email and nothing else. A chatbot that sends only the newest user message each turn has the opposite bug: the API is stateless, so it must resend every earlier turn in `messages`.

sections.heading: External storage and summarized memory
sections.body:
**External storage** keeps memory outside the context window. With the **memory tool**, Claude creates, reads, updates and deletes files under `/memories` that persist between sessions. It's client-side: Claude requests each operation and your handler executes it against storage you control, such as files, a database or cloud storage. When the tool is enabled, Claude checks its memory directory before starting a task. Your handler must reject paths outside `/memories`.

**Summarized memory** means **compaction**: when the context window nears its limit, older history is replaced with a summary. It keeps a long conversation going, but specific instructions from early in the conversation may not be preserved.

The memory tool docs suggest using both for long-running agents: compaction keeps the active context small, and memory preserves what must survive summarization.

diagram.caption: Memory tool: each session resumes from what the last one recorded.

sections.heading: Choosing a memory scope at design time
sections.body:
The choice depends on task characteristics. Ask how long the work lasts and what must survive it:

- One self-contained request: no persistent memory.
- One conversation that fits the window: in-context memory.
- Tasks requiring extensive back-and-forth: compaction, which preserves conversational flow.
- Iterative development with clear milestones: structured note-taking, notes persisted outside the context window and reloaded later.
- Knowledge that must last across conversations: external storage such as the memory tool.

In an SDK agent, put standing rules in CLAUDE.md rather than the initial prompt, because CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request. You can also add a CLAUDE.md section telling the compactor what to preserve.
sections.example: A multi-day coding project: the first session sets up a progress log and feature checklist in memory files; each later session opens by reading them, and before ending it records what was completed and what remains. A single long debugging chat instead relies on compaction.

sections.heading: Skills: reusable instructions loaded on demand
sections.body:
A **skill** is a `SKILL.md` file of instructions that Claude adds to its toolkit. Claude uses a skill when it's relevant, or you invoke it directly with `/skill-name`.

Skills don't inflate every session. In a regular session, skill **descriptions** are loaded into context so Claude knows what's available, but the **full content** loads only when the skill is invoked. This staged loading is called **progressive disclosure**, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.

Once invoked, the skill's content enters the conversation as a single message and stays there across later turns. After compaction, Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill, keeping its first 5,000 tokens, within a combined 25,000-token budget.
sections.example: An `incident-triage` skill holds a 40-line checklist. Every session carries only its one-line description, so it costs almost nothing. When someone reports an outage, Claude invokes it (or a developer types `/incident-triage`) and only then does the full checklist enter the conversation.

sections.heading: Skills vs CLAUDE.md vs in-context instructions
sections.body:
Each kind of instruction has its own place:

- **CLAUDE.md**: facts Claude should hold in **every** session, such as build commands, conventions, project layout and "always do X" rules. It loads every session; target under 200 lines.
- **Skill**: create one when you keep pasting the same instructions, checklist or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a CLAUDE.md section has grown into a procedure rather than a fact.
- **In-context instructions**: prompts are conversation-level instructions for one-off tasks. They apply only in this conversation and, in a long session, may not survive compaction. Skills load on demand, so you don't repeat the same guidance across conversations.

**Subagents and Skills.** A subagent starts with a fresh context: it doesn't see your conversation history or the skills you've already invoked. To give it a skill's content from the start, list the skill in the subagent's `skills` field, and the full content is injected at startup. That field controls preloading, not access: without it, a subagent can still invoke project, user and plugin skills through the Skill tool. To block skills entirely, omit `Skill` from its `tools` or add it to `disallowedTools`.
sections.example: Main session: you ran `/api-conventions`, then delegated to `api-developer`, which ignored them. Fix: add `skills: [api-conventions]` to `.claude/agents/api-developer.md`. In the Agent SDK, the same idea is `AgentDefinition.skills`, and unlisted skills remain invocable through the Skill tool.
